description: Hi! I’m Anirudh from Bhopal, a builder who gets way too excited about space, data and late night coding. I love turning messy science data into something people can actually see and play with. Flying solo this year for the thrill of it, but always happy to chat space with fellow hackers. Clear skies!
summary: SkyShift is a free, public web tool that turns NASA's SPHEREx all-sky survey into a time machine. Type a target name or coordinates and SkyShift pulls the real SPHEREx exposures of that patch straight from NASA's archive, stacks them into survey epochs and blinks them like a little video, the same technique that found Pluto and that Backyard Worlds volunteers use to find brown dwarfs. It then does the science on the same pixels: it finds moving and variable objects, measures distances by parallax, reads molecules and spectral types off the 0.75–5 µm spectrum of any pixel you click, checks everything against Gaia, 2MASS and WISE, and searches for distant solar-system bodies and asteroids, measuring with injected fake objects how deep each search goes. It was validated on 32 known nearby brown dwarfs and cool stars. Every view is a shareable, embeddable link.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

SkyShift is a public web tool for NASA's SPHEREx survey. Enter a target name or sky coordinates and it shows real SPHEREx infrared images of that patch blinking across survey epochs, so anything that moves or changes brightness jumps out. It then measures what it shows: motions, distances, spectra and search depth. Live demo: https://skyshift-ten.vercel.app Code (MIT): https://github.com/anirudh12032008/skyshift

HOW IT WORKS

1. Find the data: an IRSA SIA2 query lists every SPHEREx Level-2 exposure covering the position. The collection name is one config value; when IRSA replaced Quick Release 2 with Data Release 1 during the hackathon, switching was a one-line change.

2. Read only what is needed: instead of downloading ~70 MB files, SkyShift range-reads just the pixels around the target from IRSA's public S3 bucket (image, variance and flag planes).

3. Clean and align: flagged pixels are masked (and shown, never hidden); every exposure is reprojected onto one north-up 6.15 arcsec/pixel grid and background-subtracted; catalog positions are propagated by proper motion to the observation date.

4. Stack in time: exposures are grouped into survey epochs (SPHEREx revisits every ~6 months) and combined per detector with inverse-variance weights and cosmic-ray rejection.

5. Show change: blink the epoch stacks, subtract the previous epoch or the median of all epochs (movers become bright/dark pairs), or view a false-colour composite of the six detector arrays.

6. Find things automatically: sources are detected per epoch, linked across epochs and fitted with a straight-line motion, with errors calibrated on each field's static stars. Variables come from flux changes across epochs.

7. Spectra on the fly: every SPHEREx exposure is at a slightly different wavelength, so photometry on every exposure at a clicked pixel builds a 0.75-5 micron spectrum across 102 channels. SkyShift measures water, methane, CO and CO2 band depths and assigns a class.

8. Measure distance: each mover is centroided against the field's stars on the 4-5 micron detectors and fitted for position, motion and parallax using the spacecraft position from every FITS header.

9. Search for Planet X and asteroids: detections are linked along the parallax swing of a body hundreds to thousands of AU away; a shift-and-stack search co-adds every exposure along ~70,000 trial tracks to go 2-3x deeper. Each search is repeated in a form that can only find chance alignments, to count false alarms.

10. Measure completeness: fake movers, distant bodies and variables are injected into the real exposures and run through the same code, so every "nothing found" comes with the flux at which something would have been found.

RESULTS (real SPHEREx Data Release 1; every number measured by the code in the repository)

- WISE 0855: found automatically, moving 7.10 arcsec/yr westward (10.4 sigma); CatWISE2020 lists 8.09. Ours is 12% low and its parallax is not recovered, and the data show why: a Gaia star lies 3-9 arcsec from it at these epochs.

- Epsilon Indi B: 4.76 arcsec/yr (Gaia 4.68); parallax 331 +/- 54 mas, 3.0 pc (Gaia 270.7 mas, 3.69 pc); classed a methane dwarf from its spectrum alone.

- Barnard's Star: moving 12.1 arcsec/yr north (true 10.4; core saturated and flagged as such). R Draconis: x1.8 brightness change and a 269-day pulsation period from SPHEREx alone (catalogued 245.6 d).

- Validation on 32 known nearby dwarfs (M6 to Y, 8,332 exposures): 31 found; SPHEREx positions show 1.02 +/- 0.06 of the catalogued parallax; 13 of 15 T dwarfs and 0 of 13 M/L dwarfs are classed methane dwarfs from the spectrum alone.

- Planet X and asteroid searches: zero candidates. Injected bodies at 500-12,000 AU are recovered half the time at 0.16-0.19 mJy. These are calibrated nulls on 0.11 square degrees per field, not constraints on Planet X.

WHY IT MATTERS

Blinking images is how Pluto was found and how Backyard Worlds volunteers find brown dwarfs. SkyShift brings that to SPHEREx for anyone with a browser, shows data-quality problems instead of hiding them, and makes every view a shareable, embeddable link.

TOOLS

Python, FastAPI, Astropy, pyvo, NumPy, SciPy, fsspec; React + TypeScript + Vite with an HTML canvas player; Aladin Lite (CDS) for context imagery. Every measurement is tested against truth injected into a synthetic sky. Development was assisted by Claude Code (Anthropic).
